{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-vt-class-std","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"be47139baabd1aa5028509a24b8f61c300d81ea88476b1bea00f5426fe15f133","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-vt-class-std:lineage:28","source_registry_sha256":"0441bafe0dc257fd56d6bd0cd9054ad2b95889f94f5d3e5e6f98fb890bf902c4","source_liveness_sha256":"13f90fd88bb623234ea3628f2ee40ced3511148c14c82097743066ee414dd040"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Railroad crossings, pedestrians, school buses and bicyclists","heading":"C — Railroad crossings, pedestrians, school buses and bicyclists","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Railroad crossings, pedestrians, school buses and bicyclists (part one)

FACT_ID: sec07-F01 | anchor: A01
If your wheels drop off the pavement onto a low shoulder, as often happens in construction zones, reduce speed without braking and steer back onto the pavement very carefully at a slow speed [A01].
Why it matters: No braking during a shoulder drop recovery.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F02 | anchor: A01
It is against the law to drive through, around or under a closed railroad gate, and it is also illegal to pass another vehicle at a railroad crossing [A01].
Why it matters: Two absolute railroad prohibitions.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F03 | anchor: A01
Every driver must approach and cross any public or private railroad grade crossing at a safe, reduced speed [A01].
Why it matters: Speed reduction applies at private crossings too.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F04 | anchor: A01
By law a driver must stop not less than fifteen feet from the nearest rail when flashing lights, lowered gates or a flagman signal a train, when a train is seen or its whistle heard, or when a stop sign stands at the crossing [A01].
Why it matters: Fifteen feet and three triggers.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F05 | anchor: A01
After a required full stop at a crossing the vehicle may cross the tracks when it is safe, and pedestrians, bicyclists and moped riders must also obey railroad warning signals and wait until crossing is safe [A01].
Why it matters: Non drivers are bound by the same signals.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F06 | anchor: A01
If a dangerous condition exists at a rail crossing, call the number on the posted emergency sign and give the posted crossing number so the railroad can stop or reroute trains until the hazard is removed [A01].
Why it matters: The crossing number identifies the location.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F07 | anchor: A01
Drivers must watch carefully for pedestrians and be especially alert for young, elderly, disabled or intoxicated pedestrians, who are the most frequent victims of vehicle and pedestrian collisions [A01].
Why it matters: Four named high risk pedestrian groups.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F08 | anchor: A02
Many pedestrian crashes come from pedestrians entering traffic carelessly, while others come from drivers failing to yield or failing to use caution, so drive slowly and stay alert wherever pedestrians are present [A02].
Why it matters: Fault can lie on either side, but the driver must still yield.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F09 | anchor: A02
When the vehicle ahead stops for a pedestrian, do not pass it even where two lanes are provided, because passing a stopped vehicle is a frequent cause of pedestrian deaths [A02].
Why it matters: The hidden pedestrian behind a stopped car.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F10 | anchor: A02
Watch for pedestrians walking against a red light, stepping out from between parked vehicles or crossing where there is no marked crosswalk, and yield to them even when they cross carelessly [A02].
Why it matters: The driver yields regardless of the pedestrian's error.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F11 | anchor: A02
Never block a crosswalk with any part of the vehicle while stopped or waiting to turn, because that forces pedestrians to walk around you into danger [A02].
Why it matters: Partial blocking counts as blocking.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F12 | anchor: A02
Look for pedestrians every time your vehicle crosses a sidewalk or shoulder, for instance when pulling into or out of an alley, a driveway or a private road, and take extra care around playing children, who dart without checking traffic, and around elderly walkers, who may not sense the danger [A02].
Why it matters: Driveways and alleys cross pedestrian space.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F13 | anchor: A02
Do not stop to pick up hitchhikers on the interstate or its ramps [A02].
Why it matters: A short absolute rule.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F14 | anchor: A02
A pedestrian who carries a white cane or walks with a guide dog and is crossing, or waiting to cross, the street in front of you requires you to come to a stop and give up the right-of-way [A02].
Why it matters: The white cane and guide dog rule requires a stop.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F15 | anchor: A02
When turning, look for and yield to pedestrians crossing side streets, many signalized intersections light up no turn on red signs during pedestrian crossing times, and you must never turn right on a red arrow [A02].
Why it matters: Lit no turn on red signs and red arrows both bar the turn.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F16 | anchor: A02
At marked crosswalks a pedestrian sign may be placed in the road to remind drivers that they must yield to pedestrians within the crosswalk [A02].
Why it matters: In-road signs restate the yield duty.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F17 | anchor: A02
Be alert at all times for children, pedestrians and arriving or departing school buses in a school zone, where signs or flashing lights warn of the school or crossing [A02].
Why it matters: Buses are part of the school zone hazard set.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F18 | anchor: A02
Many school zones post lower speed limits that apply when flashing or when children are present, as the sign states, and children are present after school and on weekends, not only during regular school hours [A02].
Why it matters: The limit can be in force outside school hours.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F19 | anchor: A03
In residential areas and wherever children are likely, be extra careful, teach your own children pedestrian rights and duties early, and always be extra watchful when backing in or out of a driveway because children may run or play behind the vehicle [A03].
Why it matters: Backing out of a driveway is a named child hazard.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F20 | anchor: A03
Although drivers must yield to pedestrians, a pedestrian must not suddenly leave a curb or other safe place and walk into the path of a vehicle so close that it is an immediate hazard, because vehicles cannot stop at once [A03].
Why it matters: Pedestrian duty balances driver duty.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F21 | anchor: A03
Pedestrians should look both ways before crossing, obey walk and don't walk signs, not start to cross on a flashing don't walk, and may finish a crossing begun on walk during the flashing phase [A03].
Why it matters: The flashing don't walk rule has two halves.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F22 | anchor: A03
Facing a yellow or red light a pedestrian should not cross unless a walk sign shows, and where there are no pedestrian signals the pedestrian crosses when the light turns green for traffic moving the same way while watching for turning vehicles [A03].
Why it matters: Pedestrians follow the green for their direction.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F23 | anchor: A03
Pedestrians should use sidewalks where they exist, and where there are none should walk as far to the left as possible facing traffic, never on the right with their back to traffic [A03].
Why it matters: Walk left, facing traffic.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F24 | anchor: A03
Pedestrians should use crosswalks, which exist to concentrate crossings where they can be made safely, and at dawn, dusk or night should wear light colored or reflective clothing and carry a light, and should not wear headphones in busy areas so they can hear traffic [A03].
Why it matters: Visibility and hearing rules for walkers.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F25 | anchor: A03
It is against the law to pass a school bus that has stopped with its red warning lights on, from any direction [A03].
Why it matters: The core school bus rule.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F26 | anchor: A03
When a school bus is about to pick up or drop off students the driver turns on alternately flashing yellow lights and begins slowing, which means you should prepare to stop [A03].
Why it matters: Yellow flashing means a stop is coming.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F27 | anchor: A04
Once a stopped school bus activates its alternately flashing red warning lights you must stop your vehicle, and that includes inside a school yard [A04].
Why it matters: School yards are not exempt.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F28 | anchor: A04
You do not have to stop for a school bus traveling the opposite direction on a divided highway, and a concrete barrier separating traffic from the bus also removes the duty to stop [A04].
Why it matters: The two divided highway exceptions.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F29 | anchor: A04
A driver found guilty in Vermont of passing a stopped school bus with its warning lights on faces a substantial fine and five points on the driver's license [A04].
Why it matters: Five points is the stated penalty.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F30 | anchor: A04
Bicyclists have the legal right to ride on all roads except where specially prohibited, such as limited access highways like the interstate, and the same traffic rules that apply to vehicle drivers apply to them [A04].
Why it matters: Interstates are the named exception.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F31 | anchor: A04
Because bicycles are quieter and less visible, especially at night, a motorist should drive defensively around them, slow down when approaching, give plenty of room when passing, be ready to stop suddenly and not honk without good cause since the noise can startle the rider [A04].
Why it matters: Honking at a cyclist is discouraged.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F32 | anchor: A04
Bicyclists are allowed to ride as far to the left as needed for safety and may take the lane by riding toward its center because of hazards motorists cannot see or to position for the proper travel lane [A04].
Why it matters: Lane taking is legitimate, not obstruction.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F33 | anchor: A04
Drivers should recognize hazards that threaten cyclists, such as potholes, drain grates, railroad tracks and narrow bridges or roads, and give them room to maneuver around them [A04].
Why it matters: Four named cyclist hazards.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F34 | anchor: A04
A bicyclist preparing a left turn properly signals and shifts toward the left of the lane or into the turning lane, and drivers should let the rider complete that turn before overtaking [A04].
Why it matters: The cyclist's left turn position is proper, not an obstruction.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F35 | anchor: A04
When passing a bicyclist keep a gap of at least four feet between the cyclist and your vehicle's right side, and on a road too narrow for the two of you side by side, hold back until you can pass without pushing the rider off the road [A04].
Why it matters: Four feet is the passing clearance.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec07-F36 | anchor: A05
Two bicyclists riding side by side are within the law, so reduce speed, let them adjust their position if they choose, and overtake only once it is safe to do so [A05].
Why it matters: Riding two abreast is legal.
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec07-F37 | anchor: A05
An oncoming bicyclist gets the same yield from a left turning driver that an oncoming motorist gets, and riders often travel faster than they seem, so leave them room [A05].
Why it matters: Cyclists get the same left turn yield.
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec07-F38 | anchor: A05
Four common driver errors strike bicyclists: turning left without yielding to an oncoming cyclist, turning right without checking for a cyclist on the right going straight or leaving a sidewalk, entering or crossing a street without checking for a cyclist, and opening a door into a cyclist's path [A05].
Why it matters: The four named collision patterns.
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec07-F39 | anchor: A05
Bicyclists hold every right and duty of a vehicle driver without needing a license, must follow all rules of the road, may ride two abreast provided normal traffic flow is not held up, and can be ticketed and fined for traffic violations [A05].
Why it matters: No license, but full duties.
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec07-F40 | anchor: A05
A bicyclist rides with traffic on the right, stays out of a right turn lane when going straight, holds a predictable straight line instead of weaving among parked cars, may hold a narrow lane until moving right is safe, and signals turns by hand after checking the lanes are clear [A05].
Why it matters: Cyclist duties mirror driver duties.
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0042]

Misconceptions:
- If a car ahead stops in a two lane road, you may pass it in the other lane: false, never pass a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian, even with two lanes.
- A school bus with yellow flashing lights means stop immediately: false, yellow means prepare to stop; the stop is required once the red lights flash.
- You may pass a stopped school bus from the opposite direction on any road: false, the exception applies only on a divided highway or where a concrete barrier separates traffic from the bus.
- Bicyclists must stay at the far right edge at all times: false, they may ride as far left as safety needs and may take the lane.
- A right turn on red is allowed on a red arrow when clear: false, never turn right on a red arrow.

Mnemonics:
- Fifteen feet, three reasons: stop at least fifteen feet from the rail for signals, a seen or heard train, or a stop sign.
- Yellow gets ready, red gets stopped: the two school bus light phases.
- Four feet for a bike: the minimum passing clearance.
- Walk left, ride right: pedestrians face traffic, bicycles go with it.

Glossary:
- Grade crossing: a place where a road crosses railroad tracks at the same level
- Divided highway: a road whose opposing directions are separated by a median or barrier, where a school bus on the far side does not require a stop
- Taking the lane: a bicyclist riding toward the center of the lane for safety or lane positioning
- White cane rule: the duty to stop and yield to a pedestrian with a white cane or guide dog who is crossing or waiting to cross
- Low shoulder: a road edge lower than the pavement, recovered from by slowing without braking and steering back gently
